title: Five Dead After IAF An-32 Crashes at Jorhat. The Fleet Has Killed Over 100 in Four Decades.
excerpt: The Soviet-era workhorse broke apart on the runway. Its replacement was promised years ago. It still has not arrived.
body:
Five Indian Air Force personnel were killed on Saturday morning when an Antonov An-32 transport aircraft crashed while landing at the Jorhat Air Force Station in Assam. The aircraft — belonging to 43 Squadron and carrying cargo — lost control upon touchdown, skidded off the runway, hurtled across a parallel taxiway, broke apart into two segments and caught fire.

The dead have been identified as Squadron Leader Prashant Singh, Flight Lieutenant Shubham Kumar, Sergeant Jitendra Sharma, Agniveervayu Khemaram Kumawat and Agniveervayu Danish Alam. The co-pilot survived the crash with injuries and is being treated at a military hospital in Jorhat. A court of inquiry has been ordered.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh called their loss a "supreme sacrifice in the line of duty." The IAF, in its own statement, said it "deeply regrets the loss" and "stands firmly" with the bereaved families.


![Four Decades — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/b/b2/Eddie_jobson_four_decades.jpg)



> **"A joint life-extension and modernisation programme with Ukraine — valued at roughly $400 million — was supposed to add 15 years to the fleet's airworthiness."**



## An Aging Workhorse With a Deadly Record

The An-32 has been the backbone of the IAF's tactical airlift fleet since 1984. Designed by the Soviet Union's Antonov design bureau as a variant of the An-24, it was built for short, high-altitude runways and extreme weather — a turboprop with engines mounted above the wings to keep them clear of debris on unpaved strips. The rugged twin-engine transporter has kept remote military outposts across the Himalayas and the northeast supplied for over four decades, capable of carrying up to 7.5 tonnes of cargo or 50 passengers. But that very resilience has masked the toll of decades of relentless operational strain. The fleet has consumed over 100 lives in crashes during its tenure with the IAF.

The crash site itself carries grim echoes. In June 2019, another An-32 that took off from Jorhat for the advanced landing ground at Mechuka — close to the Line of Actual Control with China — went missing with 13 personnel on board. Its wreckage was found eight days later in dense forest. In July 2016, an An-32 vanished over the Bay of Bengal with 29 passengers and crew; its wreckage was located in 2024 at a depth of 3,400 metres, roughly 140 nautical miles from Chennai. In 1986, a third An-32 disappeared over the Arabian Sea during a ferry flight from Oman to Gujarat. It was never found.


![Jorhat Air Force Station — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/1d/Jorhat_Airport.jpg)


## The Replacement That Never Came

The IAF has known for years that the An-32 is on borrowed time. A joint life-extension and modernisation programme with Ukraine — valued at roughly $400 million — was supposed to add 15 years to the fleet's airworthiness. Ukraine's state-owned Antonov company upgraded 45 aircraft, and another 10 were refurbished at the IAF's Base Repair Depot in Kanpur. Then Russia annexed Crimea, Ukraine cut ties with Moscow and essential Russian components for the An-32 upgrade became unavailable. The programme stalled.

In 2022, the IAF issued a Request for Information for medium transport aircraft to replace both the An-32 and the older Il-76 fleet. But the procurement process has yet to yield a contract. India's defence acquisition cycle is notoriously slow — the light utility helicopter and basic trainer replacements each took over a decade from RFI to first delivery. The fleet, roughly 100 aircraft strong, soldiers on — with mounting maintenance costs, dwindling Ukrainian support and a safety record that grows grimmer with each passing year.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For Indian families abroad, the crash is another reminder of the human cost behind India's defence readiness — and the distance between policy announcements on indigenous defence manufacturing and the reality of ageing, Soviet-era hardware still flying daily sorties. Two of the five dead were Agniveervayus, recruits under the controversial Agnipath short-service scheme, which has drawn criticism for sending young soldiers into operational roles with limited tenures and uncertain futures.

The broader defence modernisation push — including Project Kusha, the Tejas Mark 2, the light transport aircraft programme — promises a future in which India is no longer dependent on aging foreign platforms. That future, however, did not arrive in time for the five airmen at Jorhat.
